https://nineoclock.ro/alexandru-petrescu.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Alexandru Petrescu, President of Romania’s Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF): Romania’s capital market is moving ever closer to the international investment circuit The semi-annual review carried out by the global index provider FTSE Russell brings further confirmation of the progress made by Romania’s capital market. Starting 21 September, two new companies listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange (BVB) will be included in the FTSE Global All Cap index, alongside the other Romanian firms already present in this category. Beyond the individual outcome for each issuer, this development sends an important message about the maturing of the Romanian capital market. The inclusion of new companies in international indices reflects the ability of local issuers to meet demanding criteria in terms ofliquidity, transparency, corporate governance and accessibility for global institutional investors. The presence of 10 Romanian companies in the FTSE Global All Cap and of a further 3 issuers in the FTSE Global Micro Cap marks a step forward in the process of integrating the Bucharest Stock Exchange into the international investment circuit. A developed capital market means more than the movement of share prices. It means mechanisms through which savings are turned into investment, through which companies can raise capital for growth, and through which local and international investors alike can take part in economic development. The rising number of Romanian companies included in global indices is also a signal of confidence for the market as a whole. International visibility can help attract new categories of investors, diversify companies’ sources of financing and strengthen the role of the capital market as a strategic alternative for the development of the Romanian economy. For Romania, developing the capital market remains an important objective in building a more competitive economy, one in which domestic capital and international investment can contribute together to growth and innovation. News 18 h ago Lithuanian PM appoints German military officer as adviser News 19 h ago US delivery of HIMARS delayed, says Lithuanian military chief News 21 h ago LRT English Newsletter: Raids at dawn News 1 d ago Poland would be âfirst to step inâ if Baltics attacked, says Warsaw News 1 d ago Kaunas prepares for second Pride march this Saturday News 1 d ago Lithuaniaâs Å iauliai celebrates 790th anniversary News 1 d ago Lithuanian government unveils its legislative centrepiece, â¬800m âfamily packageâ News 1 d ago US envoy John Coale âlikelyâ to visit Lithuania, PM says News 1 d ago Lithuanian power grid operator head faces dismissal after storm disruptions News 1 d ago Six Vilnius schools receive bomb threats News 1 d ago Researchers to probe found cavities in Vilnius Cathedral in search of grand dukeâs remains News 1 d ago Lithuanian Seimas to focus on security, demographics in autumn session News 2026.08.29 08:00 Lithuaniaâs storm exposed a weak link: how resilient is the mobile network? Elizabet Glazkova, LRT.lt 2026.08.29 08:00 Phone call | Shutterstock Thousands lost mobile communications after a major storm. Experts say the biggest lesson may have little to do with mobile networks themselves â and much more to do with the electricity grid. The storm that swept across Lithuania at the weekend did more than knock down trees and cut power. For tens of thousands of people, it also cut one of the most important links to the outside world: their mobile phone connection. Some residents were left without electricity or water. Fallen trees blocked roads and, in some places, people could not leave their homes. With mobile networks also disrupted, contacting relatives, emergency services or anyone else became difficult or impossible. The disruption has raised a broader question for Lithuania, a country on NATOâs eastern flank and increasingly exposed to both extreme weather and security threats: how long would the countryâs communications networks remain operational during a major emergency? Storm in Vilnius | R. Riabovas / BNS Telecoms operators reported that around 66,000 customers were affected by the storm. By Wednesday, roughly 50 mobile base stations operated by each major provider were still out of service. The worst disruption was recorded in northern, central and southern parts of the country. But experts say the storm did not reveal a fundamental failure of Lithuaniaâs mobile network. Instead, it highlighted how dependent communications are on another critical system: the electricity grid. The mobile network largely held up Lithuania has around 6,000 mobile base stations â the towers and other sites that connect mobile phones to the wider network. Around 800 stations were temporarily out of service at the height of the storm. That sounds significant, but experts point out that most were in relatively remote areas. ArtÅ«ras MedeiÅ¡is, a telecommunications specialist with three decades of experience and dean of the Faculty of Electronics at Vilnius Gediminas Technical University, said only around 2% of Lithuaniaâs population was directly affected by the mobile outages. He described the networkâs performance as broadly satisfactory, noting that the number of affected users was relatively small compared with the number of base stations that lost service. Vitas Grimaila, a researcher at Kaunas University of Technology made a similar assessment. âThe critical elements and nodes of the mobile network held up,â he said. The key point, Grimaila added, was that the core or âbackboneâ of each operatorâs network continued to function. Mobile base station | Shutterstock The stations that failed were largely part of the access network rather than the critical core infrastructure. That distinction matters. It meant Lithuaniaâs telecommunications system was not brought down as a whole, even though some communities lost mobile coverage for several days. The real problem was power According to experts and telecoms operators, the main reason mobile services failed was not physical damage to the communications equipment. It was the loss of electricity. Mobile base stations have backup batteries designed to keep them running when the power goes out. Depending on the site, those batteries can maintain services for between two and 12 hours. But the storm caused power outages that lasted much longer. Once the batteries ran out, individual base stations shut down. Nearby stations that still had electricity then had to handle more users. Some became overloaded, while others were too far away to provide adequate coverage. Repair teams also faced another problem: they had difficulty reaching damaged infrastructure because roads were blocked by fallen trees or otherwise impassable. According to Modestas RopÄ, director of next-generation networks at BitÄ Lietuva, the mobile network proved considerably more resilient than the electricity network during the storm. Around 200,000 people lost electricity, compared with roughly four times fewer people experiencing mobile communications problems. But that does not mean there is nothing to improve. For people who live in rural areas, or who happen to be in a location where mobile coverage is already weak, losing a single nearby base station can make a major difference. And in an emergency, that can become a serious problem. Should Lithuania build more mobile towers? The storm has also reignited a debate about where Lithuania should focus its investment. Storm | SIPA / Scanpix One priority is improving mobile coverage in so-called âwhite spotsâ â areas where reliable mobile service is still unavailable under normal conditions. Another is making existing infrastructure more resistant to major disruptions. MedeiÅ¡is says that having more base stations in an area reduces the risk that a single power failure will cut off a large number of people. Grimaila makes a similar argument: Lithuania should eliminate coverage gaps before focusing more heavily on strengthening the resilience and quality of the existing network. âIf a major incident occurred in an area that was a so-called white spot and residents were unable to call the emergency services, people would then be asking whether network coverage was being expanded too slowly,â Grimaila said. At the same time, simply building more towers is not enough. The network needs to be able to keep operating when electricity, roads or other infrastructure fail. One obvious solution would be to give every mobile base station its own permanent generator. But installing a generator at each of around 6,000 base stations in Lithuania, many of which are located on rooftops, water towers or other hardly accessible sites, would be impractical and extremely expensive, since installing and maintaining a diesel generator in each location would be very difficult. Mobile base station | Shutterstock Furthermore, a typical generator can consume up to 10 litres of fuel an hour. A 500-litre tank would therefore last for roughly 48 hours. During the recent storm, more than 130 base stations operated by each provider were without electricity for much longer than that. That could mean having to deliver hundreds of litres of fuel to hundreds of locations â while roads are blocked and repair crews are already stretched. As a result, experts say generators should be concentrated at the most important and vulnerable sites rather than installed everywhere. Mobile generators and regional reserves One proposal is to expand Lithuaniaâs fleet of mobile high-capacity generators. Instead of leaving a generator permanently at every tower, they could be transported quickly to locations where they are needed most. Another idea is to create regional reserves of generators and large batteries that could be deployed during major storms, disasters or other emergencies. Such reserves could potentially be used not only by telecommunications companies but also by hospitals, public authorities and other organisations providing critical services. The idea is to create a pool of emergency power that can be moved to wherever it is needed. â¬39m for a more resilient network Lithuaniaâs Communications Regulatory Authority says telecom operators have been required to invest â¬72m in expanding their networks and a further â¬39m in resilience. The resilience programme includes stronger backup power systems, additional batteries and generators, more robust network nodes and base stations, and improved emergency response and recovery capabilities. Mobile base station | J. StaceviÄius / LRT Operators are also expected to conduct regular resilience tests and simulate different emergency scenarios. The aim is that by the middle of 2028, operators should have sufficient resources to maintain and restore communications even when a large-scale incident causes prolonged electricity failures or damages a significant part of the communications infrastructure. The recent storm provided an unplanned real-world test of that resilience. Lithuania is not alone The problem is not unique to Lithuania. MedeiÅ¡is points to Australia, where major bushfires exposed a similar dependence on electricity. Australian authorities found that power failures were responsible for communications outages in 99% of cases. Australia subsequently identified several hundred strategically important mobile sites â around 2% of its total â and required operators to provide at least 12 hours of backup power at those locations. Financial support was also provided for larger batteries and, in some cases, diesel generators. Other countries are also exploring satellite communications as a backup when terrestrial networks fail. Vitas Grimaila says Lithuania could learn from the use of Starlink in parts of the United States, where satellite connectivity can provide an alternative communications route in areas affected by network outages. Such technology would not replace Lithuaniaâs mobile network. But in a serious emergency, it could provide an additional way for people in isolated areas to contact others when terrestrial infrastructure is damaged. What happens in the next major emergency? The RRT says operators already have additional measures that can be deployed during more serious emergencies, including temporary communications infrastructure, alternative transmission routes, additional generators and fuel reserves, and the redistribution of network capacity. For security reasons, details of those contingency plans are not made public. But the question raised by the storm is likely to remain relevant well beyond this particular event. As extreme weather becomes a greater challenge and countries across Europe prepare for a wider range of security threats, keeping the mobile network running may increasingly be less about the mobile network itself â and more about ensuring that the infrastructure around it can keep working when everything else starts to fail.
